title: 1.1 Small Group · Group 1
contentObjective: With my small group, I can describe the ways we are all doers of math, and compare my math story with a classmate's — one step at a time, with support.
languageObjective: I can talk through each step out loud using a sentence frame and the lesson's key words.

noticeAndWonder.context: A Ferris wheel turns slowly against the evening sky. Each car is filling with riders as the line moves forward.
noticeStarters: I notice the number of cars is ___ .
I notice each car holds about ___ .
I notice the Ferris wheel cars ___ .
wonderStarters: I wonder what math the operator ___ .

vocabulary.definition: Anyone who uses mathematical thinking — which is everyone, every day.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Cualquiera que use el pensamiento matemático, es decir, todos, todos los días.
vocabulary.example: Splitting a bill, packing a bag, keeping score.

vocabulary.definition: Your own history with mathematics — what you have done, felt, and learned so far.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Tu propia historia con las matemáticas: lo que has hecho, sentido y aprendido.
vocabulary.example: “I liked math until fractions, and now I like it again.”

vocabulary.definition: Something you already do well and can share with others.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Algo que ya haces bien y puedes compartir con otros.

vocabulary.definition: To break a number into parts that add, subtract, multiply, or divide back to it.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Separar un número en partes que se combinan para volver a formarlo.

vocabulary.definition: A reasoned answer that is close enough to be useful, without counting every one.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Una respuesta razonada, lo bastante cercana para ser útil, sin contar todo.
vocabulary.example: About how many people fit on the Ferris wheel?

launch.narrative: This is your support small group for Lesson 1.1. We're going to slow this down and build it together, one step at a time. You can ask a question any time — that's what this group is for.

conceptIntro.heading: Let's build it together — We are all doers of math
conceptIntro.intro: Before any new mathematics, the book asks a different question: where does math already live in your day? We'll walk through a worked example, try one together, then you'll try a few with hints right there when you need them.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: Everyone uses math daily. We do it differently, and sharing how we do it makes all of us better at it.

iDo.title: Watch me estimate the Ferris wheel
lines: I count the cars, then estimate how many riders fit in one car.
I do not count every person — an estimate is a reasoned answer that is close enough to be useful.
About 78.5 people can ride at one time, so I would say “about 80 people.”

weDo.title: Let's decompose 78.5 together
lines: Every one of those is the same number wearing different clothes. Find two more.
Sentence frame — say it with me: "The multiples/steps I need are ___ , and the answer is ___ ."

youDo.title: Now you try — with support
lines: Try the practice problems below. The hint button is right there whenever you get stuck — use it, that's smart.
Remember the key idea: Everyone uses math daily. We do it differently, and sharing how we do it makes all of us better at it..

explore.label: Which of these are doing math? Sort them.
categories: Most people don't call this math

cards.text: Deciding if you have enough time to walk or need to run
Splitting a pizza so everyone gets a fair share
Checking whether $12 is enough for two snacks
Guessing how many people fit on a Ferris wheel
Following a recipe and doubling it
Choosing the shorter of two lines at the store
Packing a bag so everything fits

explore.instructions: Quick warm-up together: Every card belongs on the left. That is the point of this lesson — you are already doing far more math than you get credit for. After sorting, say which one surprised you.

diagram.title: Ferris Wheel Estimate: Cars to Riders
diagram.caption: Each group of 5 cars carries about 20 riders; four groups make 20 cars and about 80 riders, which is why 20 × 4 is a reasonable estimate.

connect.scenario: What we believe about ourselves, about others, and about what we are learning shapes us. Your classmate has a math story too, and it is not the same as yours.
connect.promptQuestion: What do you believe are your math strengths, and which area do you most want to grow this year?
connect.prompt: Name one math ___ you already have and one area you want to ___ . Then name one thing you learned from a ___ 's math story.

check.stem: The lesson says, “What we believe about ourselves, about others, and about what we are learning shapes us.” Why does the Strengths Inventory ask you to name a growth area, not only a strength?
choices: Naming what you want to grow shapes how you approach learning all year, just as naming a strength does
Growth areas are only for students who are behind in math
The growth area replaces the strength, since you can only claim one
Naming a growth area has nothing to do with your beliefs about yourself
check.explanation: A growth area is a belief about your future the same way a strength is a belief about your present — both shape learning, so the lesson asks for both, not one instead of the other.

check.stem: One student's math story says she liked math more once she started drawing problems; another's says he liked it more once he memorized steps. What is the point of hearing a classmate's story that is DIFFERENT from yours?
choices: It shows there is more than one valid way to be a doer of math, and you might borrow a new strategy
Whichever method is faster is the “right” one, so you should switch to it
If a classmate's story differs from yours, one of you must be doing math wrong
It doesn't matter — you only need to hear stories similar to your own
check.explanation: The lesson's summary says we all do math differently and learning about each other's strengths helps everyone grow — differences are the point, not a sign that someone is wrong.

check.stem: Which of these is the BEST example of a specific math strength for the Connect prompt?
choices: “I can explain my thinking out loud so others can follow my steps”
“I'm good at math”
“I got an A last year”
“Math is easy for me”
check.explanation: The check says a complete answer names a SPECIFIC strength, not a vague self-assessment like “I'm good at math” or “math is easy,” and not an unrelated fact like a grade.

connect.modelAnswer: One of my math strengths is explaining my thinking out loud, because I can usually say why an answer makes sense. I want to grow at not giving up when a problem takes more than one try. From my partner's story I learned that she liked math more when she got to draw the problem, which I had never tried.

diagram.title: Riders per Ferris Wheel Turn (6 Turns in One Hour)
diagram.caption: Six turns carry 78, 80, 76, 82, 74, and 78 riders — 468 riders in the hour, which is why about 78 riders a turn is a reasonable estimate.

approaching.stem: About how many people can ride the Ferris wheel at one time if it has 20 cars that each hold about 4 people?
choices: About 80
About 24
About 5
About 400
approaching.explanation: 20 cars with about 4 riders each is 20 × 4, which is about 80 people.
choiceFeedback: That adds 20 + 4 instead of multiplying.
That divides 20 by 4 instead of multiplying.
That multiplies as if each car held 20 people.
hints: How many groups are there, and how big is each group?
20 groups of 4.
Multiply 20 × 4.
approaching.stemEs: ¿Aproximadamente cuántas personas pueden subir a la rueda de la fortuna a la vez si tiene 20 cabinas y cada una lleva unas 4 personas?
approaching.explanationEs: 20 carros con unos 4 pasajeros cada uno es 20 × 4, que son unas 80 personas.

approaching.stem: Which of these is a correct way to decompose 78.5?
approaching.explanation: 70 + 8.5 = 78.5. Decomposing means the parts must add back to the original number.
hints: Add each option and see what you get.
The parts must total 78.5 exactly.
Add the two parts in each choice. Which total lands exactly on 78.5?
approaching.stemEs: ¿Cuál de estas es una manera correcta de descomponer 78.5?
approaching.explanationEs: 70 + 8.5 = 78.5. Descomponer significa que las partes deben sumar de nuevo el número original.

approaching.explanation: 80 − 1.5 = 78.5. Decomposing can use subtraction, not only addition.
choiceFeedback: 80 + 1.5 = 81.5 — that moves the wrong direction.
hints: Start at 80. How far down is 78.5?
Check your subtraction against each choice: which one starts above 78.5 and takes away exactly that gap?
approaching.explanationEs: 80 − 1.5 = 78.5. Descomponer puede usar resta, no solo suma.

approaching.stem: Name one way you used math outside of school this week.
approaching.modelAnswer: I used math when I figured out I needed to leave by 7:40 to catch the bus at 7:55.
sentenceStems: It was math because I had to ___ .
approaching.stemEs: Nombra una manera en que usaste matemáticas fuera de la escuela esta semana.

approaching.stem: What does it mean to ESTIMATE how many people are on the Ferris wheel?
choices: Give a reasoned answer that is close enough to be useful
Count every single person exactly
Guess any number at random
Refuse to answer without more data
approaching.explanation: An estimate is reasoned, not random, and it does not require counting every one.
choiceFeedback: Counting every person exactly is not estimating — that is an exact count.
A random guess uses no reasoning, so it is not an estimate.
Estimating is what you do precisely when you cannot count them all.
hints: Is an estimate exact?
Is an estimate random?
It sits between those two.
approaching.stemEs: ¿Qué significa ESTIMAR cuántas personas hay en la rueda de la fortuna?
approaching.explanationEs: Una estimación es razonada, no al azar, y no requiere contar cada uno.
choicesEs: Dar una respuesta razonada que sea lo bastante cercana para ser útil
Negarse a responder sin más datos

approaching.stem: Tell one thing you already do well in math.
approaching.modelAnswer: I am good at checking my answer to see whether it makes sense.
sentenceStems: One thing I do well is ___ .
approaching.stemEs: Di una cosa que ya haces bien en matemáticas.

onLevel.stem: Which decomposition of 78.5 uses multiplication correctly?
onLevel.explanation: 39.25 × 2 = 78.5, so halving and doubling is another way to break the number apart.
choiceFeedback: 78.5 × 2 = 157, which doubles the number instead of rebuilding it.
39 × 2 = 78, which is close but not 78.5.
hints: What is half of 78.5?
Half of 78.5 is 39.25.
Two of those halves rebuild it.
onLevel.stemEs: ¿Cuál descomposición de 78.5 usa la multiplicación correctamente?
onLevel.explanationEs: 39.25 × 2 = 78.5, así que sacar la mitad y duplicar es otra manera de descomponer el número.

onLevel.stem: A Ferris wheel holds about 78 riders per turn and makes 6 turns an hour. About how many riders per hour?
choices: About 468
About 84
About 13
About 780
onLevel.explanation: 78 riders on each of 6 turns is 78 × 6 = 468 riders in an hour.
choiceFeedback: That adds 78 + 6 instead of multiplying.
That divides 78 by 6 instead of multiplying.
That multiplies by 10 instead of 6.
hints: Each turn carries a full load. How many turns?
6 turns of 78 riders.
onLevel.stemEs: Una rueda de la fortuna lleva unos 78 pasajeros por vuelta y da 6 vueltas por hora. ¿Aproximadamente cuántos pasajeros por hora?
onLevel.explanationEs: 78 pasajeros en cada una de 6 vueltas es 78 × 6 = 468 pasajeros en una hora.

onLevel.stem: Describe three different situations where you use math in your life. Say how the math is the SAME in each one.
onLevel.modelAnswer: I use math when I cook, when I skate, and when I save money. In all three I am comparing amounts to decide whether I have enough.
sentenceStems: I use math when I ___ , when I ___ , and when I ___ .
onLevel.stemEs: Describe tres situaciones distintas en las que usas matemáticas en tu vida. Di en qué se PARECEN las matemáticas en cada una.

onLevel.stem: Which statement matches this lesson's big idea?
choices: Everyone is a doer of math, and we do it in different ways
Only people who are fast at math are doers of math
Math only counts when it happens in a classroom
There is one right way to think about a math problem
onLevel.explanation: The lesson's whole point is that everyone already does math, differently, and sharing those differences helps everyone.
choiceFeedback: Speed is not what makes someone a doer of math.
The Ferris wheel, the recipe and the bus are all outside a classroom.
Different approaches are exactly what makes sharing worthwhile.
hints: What did the sorting activity show?
Every card belonged in 'this is doing math'.
And people sorted their reasons differently.
onLevel.stemEs: ¿Cuál enunciado coincide con la gran idea de esta lección?
onLevel.explanationEs: Toda la idea de la lección es que todos ya hacemos matemáticas, de maneras distintas, y compartir esas diferencias ayuda a todos.
choicesEs: Todos hacemos matemáticas, y lo hacemos de maneras distintas
Solo las personas rápidas en matemáticas hacen matemáticas
Las matemáticas solo cuentan cuando ocurren en un salón de clases
Hay una sola manera correcta de pensar un problema de matemáticas

onLevel.stem: Ask a classmate about their math story. What is one way their story is DIFFERENT from yours?
onLevel.modelAnswer: My partner said she liked math most when she could draw the problem, but I usually want to write the numbers first. We get to the same answer starting from different places.
sentenceStems: My partner's story is different because ___ .
onLevel.stemEs: Pregúntale a un compañero sobre su historia matemática. ¿En qué se DIFERENCIA su historia de la tuya?

onLevel.stem: You estimate 80 riders and the true count is 78. Was your estimate useful?
choices: Yes — it was close enough to plan with
No — an estimate is only useful if it is exact
No — you should never estimate
Yes — because any answer is fine
onLevel.explanation: 80 and 78 are close enough for planning, which is exactly what an estimate is for.
choiceFeedback: Exactness is what a count is for, not an estimate.
Estimating is a real mathematical tool, used constantly.
Not any answer — a good estimate has reasoning behind it.
hints: How far off were you?
Off by 2 out of about 80.
Close enough to be useful.
onLevel.stemEs: Estimas 80 pasajeros y el conteo real es 78. ¿Fue útil tu estimación?
onLevel.explanationEs: 80 y 78 están lo bastante cerca para planear, que es exactamente para lo que sirve una estimación.
choicesEs: Sí — estuvo lo bastante cerca para poder planear
No — una estimación solo es útil si es exacta

practice.commonMistake: Believing that 'doing math' only counts when it happens on paper in a classroom.

exitTicket.stem: Quick check — you've got this: Which statement best shows what this lesson means by “we are all doers of math”?
choices: Everyone uses mathematical thinking daily, in different ways, and sharing those ways helps us grow
Everyone gets the same score if they try hard enough
Everyone must solve problems the same way to be correct
Only the fastest students are really doing math
exitTicket.explanation: The summary makes three claims: everyone does math, we do it differently, and sharing our strengths helps all of us.
hints: Look back at the Summarize slide.
It has three parts: everyone, differently, sharing.
Which option keeps all three?

turnAndTalk.question: The Ferris wheel has 20 cars, and you estimated about 4 riders fit in each car. Why is 20 × 4 an estimate and not an exact count?
turnAndTalk.kernel: The book estimates about 80 riders by multiplying 20 cars by about 4 riders per car, without counting every person.

stems.en: This is an estimate because ___, not an exact count.
stems.es: Esto es una estimación porque ___, no un conteo exacto.

turnAndTalk.extend: If you later found out each car actually holds 5 riders, would your estimate of 80 still be useful? Justify your answer using the new total.
extendStems: With 5 riders per car, the new estimate would be ___, so my first estimate was ___.
The estimate is still useful because ___.

turnAndTalk.question: You sorted cards like 'splitting a pizza fairly' and 'choosing the shorter line' as doing math. What do all eight cards have in common that makes them math, even though none of them looks like a worksheet?
turnAndTalk.kernel: Every card on the board describes a real decision — like splitting a pizza or checking if $12 covers two snacks — that uses reasoning or comparison, even without a written equation.

stems.en: These are all math because each one involves ___.
stems.es: Todas estas son matemáticas porque cada una involucra ___.

stems.en: The card that surprised me most was ___ because ___.
stems.es: La tarjeta que más me sorprendió fue ___ porque ___.

turnAndTalk.extend: Could you find an example from YOUR day this week that belongs on the 'This is doing math' side of the board? Defend why it counts.
extendStems: My example is ___, and it counts as math because ___.
It is like the pizza card because both involve ___.

turnAndTalk.question: The lesson says naming a growth area matters just as much as naming a strength. Why might sharing your growth area with a classmate actually help both of you this year?
turnAndTalk.kernel: The Strengths Inventory asks students to name one math strength AND one area to grow, plus one thing learned from a classmate's math story.

stems.en: My math strength is ___, and the area I want to grow is ___.
stems.es: Mi fortaleza en matemáticas es ___, y el área que quiero mejorar es ___.

stems.en: Hearing my partner's story helped me because ___.
stems.es: Escuchar la historia de mi compañero me ayudó porque ___.

turnAndTalk.extend: Is it possible for your growth area to become a strength by the end of the year? What would have to happen for that to be true?
extendStems: My growth area could become a strength if I ___.

turnAndTalk.question: One practice problem asked about how many people ride the Ferris wheel if it has 20 cars that each hold about 4 people. What strategy did you use to find about 80?
turnAndTalk.kernel: 20 cars of about 4 riders each is 20 × 4, which is about 80 people — a strategy of multiplying equal groups.

stems.en: I knew my answer was reasonable because ___.
stems.es: Supe que mi respuesta era razonable porque ___.

turnAndTalk.extend: How would you help a classmate who added 20 + 4 instead of multiplying? Use one vocabulary word.
extendStems: I would tell them to ___ because ___.
Adding instead of multiplying is a mistake because ___.

parallelPractice.stem: Divide 252 by 6. Give the quotient and remainder.
hints: Re-read the question. What exactly is it asking you to find?
Use the visual model, then complete one step at a time.
Start like this: 6 fits into 252 about 42 times.
parallelPractice.explanation: 6 fits into 252 about 42 times. Multiply back: 6 × 42 = 252. The amount left is 0.
parallelPractice.stemEs: Divide 252 entre 6. Escribe el cociente y el residuo.
hintsEs: Vuelve a leer la pregunta. ¿Qué te pide encontrar exactamente?
Usa el modelo visual y completa un paso a la vez.
Empieza así: 6 cabe en 252 aproximadamente 42 veces.
parallelPractice.explanationEs: 6 cabe en 252 aproximadamente 42 veces. Multiplica para comprobar: 6 × 42 = 252. La cantidad que sobra es 0.
